description: Three-panel composite figure of tensile-test results for a Fe–20Mn–6Al–0.6C–0.15Si austenitic low-density steel at three deformation temperatures. (a) Engineering stress (MPa, axis 0–1400, ticks every 200) versus engineering strain (0–70, ticks every 10) with three curves legend-labelled "25 °C" (grey), "-77 °C" (red) and "-196 °C" (blue); the -196 °C curve reaches the highest stress and the largest strain (beyond 65), the 25 °C curve the lowest (ends near strain 33, stress between the 600 and 800 MPa gridlines). (b) True stress or work hardening rate (MPa, 0–2500) versus true strain (0.0–0.5): solid lines are true stress–true strain curves and dashed lines the corresponding work hardening rate for the same three temperatures; arrows and the annotation "σtrue=dσtrue/dεtrue" mark the necking intersections, highest for the -196 °C pair. (c) Two stacked sub-panels sharing a tensile-temperature axis (°C, -200 to 50): upper plots TE (blue) and UE (red) elongation (%, 0–70), both increasing as temperature decreases; lower plots UTS (blue) and YS (red) strength (MPa, 400–1400) with printed linear fits "UTS=813.0-2.36*T" and "YS=474.6-2.05*T", all points carrying error bars. Together the panels show that lowering temperature raises strength and elongation simultaneously, i.e. a negative temperature dependence of strength, with the necking analysis in (b) accounting for the extended ductility.

observations.observation: Panel (a) contains three engineering stress–strain curves whose legend entries are exactly '25 °C', '-77 °C' and '-196 °C'.

In (a) the -196 °C curve extends furthest along the strain axis (beyond the 60 gridline) and reaches the highest engineering stress (above the 1200 MPa gridline), while the 25 °C curve terminates earliest (near strain 33).

Panel (b) overlays solid true stress–true strain curves and dashed work hardening rate curves for the same three temperatures, and is annotated 'σtrue=dσtrue/dεtrue' with arrows at the intersections identifying the necking points.
In (b) the necking intersection for the -196 °C pair lies at the highest stress and true strain, and that for 25 °C at the lowest stress and strain.
Panel (c) upper sub-panel plots elongation (%) 0–70 versus tensile temperature (°C) with TE (blue) above UE (red); both increase monotonically as temperature decreases from RT to -196 °C.
Panel (c) lower sub-panel prints the linear-fit equations 'UTS=813.0-2.36*T' and 'YS=474.6-2.05*T' for the strength data.
Every data point in (c) carries error bars, indicating scatter in the elongation and strength measurements.

The caption states Fig. 2 presents tensile test results at -196 °C, -77 °C and RT and that the panels are (a) engineering stress-strain curves, (b) true stress-strain and work hardening rate curves, (c) elongation and strength varying with temperature.

The citing text states the work hardening rate decreases dramatically with strain at the initial stage of deformation, corresponding to the elastic-to-plastic transition, and then decreases near-linearly at -77 and -196 °C but continuously at RT.
The citing text states that as deformation temperature decreases the work hardening rate increases, indicating a negative temperature dependence of strength.
The citing text defines the necking point as the true strain at which true stress equals the work hardening rate (dσtrue/dεtrue).
The citing text states that total elongation (TE) and uniform elongation (UE) increase with decreasing temperature and that decreasing temperature leads to a linear increase in both YS and UTS.
The citing text links the increasing strength and elongation in Fig. 2c to decreasing stacking fault energy promoting dislocation planar glide as temperature falls from RT to -196 °C.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress (MPa, 0–1400) vs engineering strain (0–70) curves for 25 °C (grey), -77 °C (red) and -196 °C (blue). Strength and strain-to-fracture both rise as temperature falls: the 25 °C curve terminates near strain 33 at ~760 MPa, the -77 °C curve near strain 59 at ~990 MPa, the -196 °C curve beyond strain 65 near 1280 MPa.

True stress or work hardening rate (MPa, 0–2500) vs true strain (0.0–0.5). Solid lines = true stress–true strain; dashed lines = work hardening rate, for 25 °C, -77 °C and -196 °C. Annotation σtrue=dσtrue/dεtrue with arrows marks the necking point of each pair; the -196 °C pair intersects at the highest stress and strain.

Two stacked plots vs tensile temperature (°C, -200 to 50). Upper: elongation (%) 0–70 with TE (blue) and UE (red) curves rising as temperature decreases. Lower: strength (MPa) 400–1400 with UTS (blue) and YS (red) points, error bars, and printed linear-fit labels UTS=813.0-2.36*T and YS=474.6-2.05*T.
